input:
This executive summary looks at delivery performance at a contract packaging firm and at whether a new scheduling system should be installed. The firm operates 3 plants and has revenue of $94 million per year. The evidence base for this summary is the firm's order records for 12 months, covering a total of 13805 orders.

Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery was 84%, which is well below the target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.1 million last year, which represents an increase of 26% compared with the year before. The order backlog currently stands at 3.6 weeks, compared with 2 weeks a year ago, so the position has deteriorated on several measures at the same time.

It is worth noting that the problem is concentrated in one location: Plant 2 accounts for 60% of all late orders. A scheduling system covering all plants has been quoted at $264k, while Plant 2 alone would cost $141k. An internal estimate suggests that the overtime reduction at Plant 2 could be in the region of 15-20% in the first year, although it should be emphasised that this is an internal estimate rather than a vendor figure. The recommendation under consideration is therefore to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until the Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.

It should also be noted that the recommendation is a staged one rather than a partial one, in the sense that the other plants are not being removed from the programme; rather, their installation is deferred until evidence from the first installation is available, at which point a further decision can be taken in the light of that evidence.

Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first; the other plants are held until the Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.

The firm runs 3 plants with revenue of $94 million per year. The evidence base is order records for 12 months, covering 13805 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 84%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.1 million last year, up 26% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.6 weeks, against 2 weeks a year ago.

Late delivery is concentrated: Plant 2 accounts for 60% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $264k; Plant 2 alone is $141k. An internal estimate puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year; the estimate is internal, not a vendor figure, and it is the only quantified benefit in the case. The sequence spends the smaller sum first and tests the benefit where late orders concentrate. The backlog and the overtime bill are the two figures the programme is expected to move, and both are at their weakest where the system would go in first. If the reported results hold, the case for the remaining plants rests on measured delivery and overtime figures from the firm's own operation rather than on the estimate alone, and the decision to extend is taken on that evidence.

The recommendation is staged rather than partial: the held plants are not descoped, and their installation follows on the reported result without a second case being built. What the staging buys is a decision point with evidence in hand. What it costs is time, since the held plants run on the present arrangements while the first installation is assessed, and the overtime and backlog figures for those plants are not expected to improve in the interval.
